say: This is the Dutch national flag problem: one pass with three pointers sorts the zeros, ones and twos.

With a prefix sum array, any range sum is the difference of two entries.

A 2D prefix sum gives any rectangle's sum in O(1) with inclusion-exclusion.
To merge intervals, I sort them by start and extend the last one while the next one starts no later than it ends.
A sweep line over the sorted start and end events tells me how many meetings overlap at once.
A subarray has to be contiguous, unlike a subsequence.

A trie, usually pronounced like try, stores words by prefix, so a lookup costs only the word's length.
For serialization, I write the tree in preorder with a marker for each null child.
The iterator does its work in hasNext, so next only returns the value it found.
With union-find, I join the two ends of each edge, and an edge whose ends are already connected closes a cycle.
Path compression flattens the tree during find, so later finds are almost constant time.
Union by size hangs the smaller tree under the larger one, which keeps the trees shallow.
A segment tree supports range sum queries and point updates in O(log n).
With lazy propagation, a range update stops at fully covered nodes and pushes the change down later.
A Fenwick tree, also called a binary indexed tree, handles prefix sums with updates in O(log n).
A sparse table answers range minimum queries in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing.
In Java I'd use a TreeMap to find the floor and ceiling keys in O(log n).
A dynamic array doubles its capacity when it fills up.

In a binary tree, every node has at most two children.

With V vertices and E edges, BFS runs in O(V plus E).
The prerequisites form a directed graph, with an edge from each course to the courses it unlocks.
In a weighted graph, the path with the fewest edges isn't always the cheapest.

A node with an in-degree of zero has no prerequisites left, so it goes into the queue.

Each DFS from an unvisited node covers exactly one connected component.

With equal edge costs BFS gives the shortest path; with non-negative weights I need Dijkstra.

A minimum spanning tree connects all n nodes with n minus one edges of the least total weight.

say: Kadane's algorithm either extends the current run or restarts at the current element.
With state machine DP, each day has a holding state and a not-holding state.

Weighted interval scheduling sorts the jobs by end time and binary searches for the last compatible one.
In tree DP, each node returns two values: the best with it taken and the best without it.

In this game DP, each range stores the best score difference the player to move can force.

zh: 第一个大于等于 x 的位置
say: Lower bound returns the first index whose value is at least the target.
Backtracking builds the answer one choice at a time and undoes each choice after the recursive call.

With the candidates sorted, I can prune the rest of the loop once the sum passes the target.
Placing one queen per row shrinks the search space to n choices per row.

A greedy choice works here: always take the meeting that ends first.
An exchange argument proves it: swapping an optimal answer's first pick for the earliest-ending interval never makes it worse.
Interval scheduling sorts by end time and keeps each interval that starts after the last kept one ends.
With bit manipulation I can test the k-th bit using a shift and an AND.
Since a XOR a is zero, XOR-ing every number leaves the one that appears once.
I use a bitmask to record which letters a word contains, one bit per letter.
x AND negative x isolates the lowest set bit, which is how a Fenwick tree jumps.
A left shift by one doubles the number, as long as it doesn't overflow.
In two's complement, negative x equals NOT x plus one.
Popcount, the number of set bits, is a single built-in call in most languages.
Fast exponentiation squares the base every round, so it needs only O(log n) multiplications.
I take the result modulo ten to the ninth plus seven after every addition.
The modulus is prime, so the modular inverse of a is a to the power of the modulus minus two.
The Euclidean algorithm finds the GCD in a logarithmic number of steps.
The least common multiple is a divided by the GCD, times b; dividing first avoids overflow.
The sieve of Eratosthenes crosses out the multiples of each prime and finds every prime up to n in O(n log log n).
Trial division up to the square root of n gives the prime factorization.
The binomial coefficient n choose k counts the ways to pick k items out of n.
By the pigeonhole principle, n plus one numbers from one to n must contain a duplicate.
By inclusion-exclusion, the numbers divisible by two or three are the two counts minus the numbers divisible by six.
Every move changes the sum by an even number, so its parity never changes and an odd target can't be reached from an even start.
For ceiling division with integers, I compute a plus b minus one, divided by b.
Reservoir sampling keeps the i-th item with probability one over i, so every item is equally likely to be chosen.
